title: References
summary: A **reference** is a second name for an existing variable. Pass by reference to let a function change the caller's variable. Pass by **const reference** to avoid copying something large.
markdown:
## A second name for the same box ```cpp #include int main() { int x{ 5 }; int& ref{ x }; // ref is another name for x ref = 10; std::cout << x << '\n'; // 10 return 0; } ``` ``` x ─┐ ├──▶ ┌──────┐ ref ─┘ │ 10 │ one box, two names └──────┘ ``` `int&` reads "reference to int". There is no second box. Anything done to `ref` is done to `x`. | Rule | Consequence | |---|---| | A reference must be initialized | `int& r;` does not compile | | It cannot be made to refer to something else | `ref = y;` copies the **value** of `y` into `x` | | It always refers to something | There is no "empty" reference | ## Pass by value and pass by reference This is what references are for. ```cpp #include void addOneByValue(int n) { ++n; // changes the copy } void addOneByReference(int& n) { ++n; // changes the caller's variable } int main() { int score{ 5 }; addOneByValue(score); std::cout << score << '\n'; // 5 addOneByReference(score); std::cout << score << '\n'; // 6 return 0; } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph V["Pass by value"] direction TB m1["main: score is 5"] -->|"a copy is made"| f1["n: 5 becomes 6"] f1 -.->|"the copy is discarded"| m1b["score is still 5"] end subgraph R["Pass by reference"] direction TB m2["main: score is 5"] -->|"n is another name for score"| f2["score: 5 becomes 6"] f2 --> m2b["score is 6"] end ``` ## Pass by const reference Copying an `int` costs nothing. Copying a `std::string` of a million characters copies a million characters. A **const reference** gives the function access to the original with a promise not to change it. ```cpp void printReport(const std::string& report) { std::cout << report << '\n'; } ``` No copy is made, and the compiler rejects any attempt to modify `report` inside the function. ### Choosing a parameter type ```mermaid flowchart TD Q1{"Must the function
change the caller's object?"} -- yes --> A["T&"] Q1 -- no --> Q2{"Is it cheap to copy?"} Q2 -- "yes: int, double, char, bool,
enums, std::string_view" --> B["T (by value)"] Q2 -- "no: std::string, containers,
most structs" --> C["const T&"] ``` This decision comes up for every function you will ever write. Learn the three outcomes. ## Returning more than one value A function has one return value. Reference parameters, often called **out-parameters**, are one way round that: ```cpp void minMax(int a, int b, int& outMin, int& outMax) { outMin = a < b ? a : b; outMax = a < b ? b : a; } int low{}; int high{}; minMax(8, 3, low, high); // low is 3, high is 8 ``` It works, but nothing at the call site shows that `low` and `high` will be changed. Returning a struct is usually clearer: [[4.06 Structs]]. ## Dangling references A reference is only valid while the thing it refers to exists. ```cpp int& broken() { int local{ 5 }; return local; // local is destroyed here } ``` The caller receives a reference to a variable that no longer exists. Using it is undefined behaviour. A reference in this state is said to be **dangling**. > [!danger] Never return a reference to a local variable > Return by value instead. Returning a reference is only safe when the object outlives the function call, for example a parameter that was itself passed by reference. ## What a reference can bind to | Declaration | Allowed? | Why | |---|---|---| | `int& r{ x };` | Yes | `x` is a variable | | `int& r{ 5 };` | No | `5` is a temporary value with no lasting home | | `const int& r{ 5 };` | Yes | A const reference may bind to a temporary and keeps it alive | This is why `const std::string&` parameters accept string literals and results of expressions. Two terms you will meet often from here on: | Term | Roughly | Examples | |---|---|---| | **lvalue** | Something with a name and a lasting location | `x`, `name`, `values[0]` | | **rvalue** | A temporary value | `5`, `x + 1`, the result of a function returning by value | They matter a great deal in [[7.05 Move Semantics]]. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? After `int& r{ a }; r = b;`, what has changed? + `a` now holds the value of `b`; `r` still refers to `a` - `r` now refers to `b`, and `a` is unchanged - `b` now holds the value of `a` - Nothing; a reference cannot be assigned to > A reference cannot be re-aimed. Assigning to `r` assigns to `a`, the variable it names. ? What is the best parameter type for a function that only reads a `std::string`? - `std::string`, so the function gets its own copy - `std::string&`, so no copy is made + `const std::string&`, or `std::string_view` - `std::string*`, so the caller can pass `nullptr` > A const reference (or a `std::string_view`) avoids the copy and guarantees the function cannot change the caller's string. ? Why is returning a reference to a local variable dangerous? - It makes a copy that is slow to create - The compiler cannot work out the return type + The local is destroyed when the function returns, so the reference dangles - The caller can change the local after the function ends > Once the function returns, the local no longer exists, so using the reference is undefined behaviour. ? Why can `const int&` bind to `5` when `int&` cannot? - `5` is too small to need a non-const reference - `int&` can only bind to variables declared `const` - They both can; `int&` just gives a warning + A const reference may bind to a temporary; a non-const one may not > A non-const reference promises it can change what it refers to, which makes no sense for a literal. A const reference can safely hold on to a temporary. ```
ideas:
1. Write `void swapInts(int& a, int& b)` and test it.
2. Write `void toUpperInPlace(std::string& text)` using a loop over the indexes.
3. Write `void stats(int a, int b, int c, double& average, int& largest)`.

cards.q: After `int& r{ a }; r = b;`, what has changed?
cards.a:
`a` now holds the value of `b`; `r` still refers to `a`

A reference cannot be re-aimed. Assigning to `r` assigns to `a`, the variable it names.

cards.q: What is the best parameter type for a function that only reads a `std::string`?
cards.a:
`const std::string&`, or `std::string_view`

A const reference (or a `std::string_view`) avoids the copy and guarantees the function cannot change the caller's string.

cards.q: Why is returning a reference to a local variable dangerous?
cards.a:
The local is destroyed when the function returns, so the reference dangles

Once the function returns, the local no longer exists, so using the reference is undefined behaviour.

cards.q: Why can `const int&` bind to `5` when `int&` cannot?
cards.a:
A const reference may bind to a temporary; a non-const one may not

A non-const reference promises it can change what it refers to, which makes no sense for a literal. A const reference can safely hold on to a temporary.
